newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. hospitals seen coping with deregulation - S&P.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. hospitals seen coping with deregulation - S&P.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp on Monday said that hospitals in New York State, which at the start of the year deregulated rates, are not likely to suffer severely enough to trigger downgrades.

"Standard and Poor's concludes that wholesale rating changes in New York debt are unlikely and, over time, there is reason to believe that some credit quality will improve. The state's long history of rate regulation held many industry changes at bay, but absent regulation, New York will quickly catch up to the rest of the country," S&P said in Monday's edition of CreditWeek Municipal.

To succeed with deregulation, the rating agency said hospitals will have to control costs, the first most important step. It noted the state's hospitals costs run above their peers, mainly because the time a patient stays in the hospital is two days higher than the national average.

Cost cutting likely will drive more consolidations and joint ventures among hospitals, produce improved management, financial and clinical information systems, develop strategies for primary care phsysicians, and for some hospitals, spur management and board changes.
The high level of unionized employees is another cost issue, but the rating agency noted it already was seeing speeded-up cost cuts, mergers and joint ventures.
Out of 16 unenhanced ratings, which add up to nearly $500 million in outstanding debt that largely was issued through local authorities, 10 fell in the triple BBB category, S&P said.
The other six are split equally between the single A category and speculative grade. In contrast, the nation averages 44 percent of ratings in the single A category.

The rating agency rates fairly few unenhanced bond issues in New York because the major, statewide issuers, such as the Dormitory Authority, are required to get credit enhancement for entities that cannot get a single A-plus rating or better.

The Federal Housing Authority insures more than 50 mortgage loans totaling about $3.4 billion in outstanding, long-term debt, the rating agency said, noting that the Dormitory Authority has control of about $60 million that could be used to aid hospitals that have trouble adjusting to the deregulated arena.

The new system lets hospitals negotiate all rates, except Medicare and fee-for-service, which makes cost base, service mix, geographical location and market position more important. While financial margins likely will be compressed, experience in other states shows that as hospitals cut costs and strengthen their negotiating position, profitablity rebounds.
The rating agency made the following points:
--Funding for bad debt and charity care is level at $738 million, but financially distressed hospitals will be at increased risk as their special status is phased out.
--State funding for graduate school education will be cut by almost $500 million to $1.4 billion, which could cause universities and medical schools to change their minds about owning hospitals.
--Funding for public hospitals will have their subsidies held constant at 1996 levels.

--The Dormitory Authority may have as much as $100 million to aid hospitals that need to make big changes under deregulation, though the money will not be available for debt service and the total when compared to the number of hospitals in the state is very small.

--Gov George Pataki's new budget proposes over $3 billion of funding cutbacks or additional fees for Medicaid, including extending last year's funding cuts, which sunset on March 31. If approved, such large reductions "would certainly add a significant burden to hospitals struggling to reinvent themselves under deregulation and could lead to more downgrades for Medicaid dependent facilities," the rating agency said.

--Hospitals would bear the brunt of such cuts, over $1.8 billion in total funds, and if the state gets Washington's approval to move 3.5 million Medicaid recipients to managed care plans by year-end, it will heighten competition for more facilities for less Medicaid dollars.
